title: Use Case Diagrams
body:
Later stage in analysis
Good for communicating with non-technical people

A use case diagram shows **who uses the system and what they can do with it**, and nothing
else. Three parts:

- **Actors**, drawn as stick figures, outside the system boundary. A person in a role, or
  another system. The same human can be two actors if they act in two roles.
- **Use cases**, drawn as ovals inside the boundary. One goal the actor can accomplish,
  named as a verb phrase: *place order*, *cancel booking*, *reset password*.
- **The system boundary**, the box around the use cases. Drawing it is the point: it settles
  what is being built and what is merely talked to, which is the scope decision made in
  [[Problem Recognition]].

What it deliberately leaves out is the whole reason it is readable: no sequence, no
conditions, no data, no screens. It answers "what is this system for and who for" in one
picture. The step-by-step detail belongs in the written use case and in the
[[Specification]].

Why they land late in analysis: they need the actors and the boundary already worked out, so
they come after [[Problem Recognition]] and [[Evaluation and Synthesis]]. And their audience
is the stakeholder, so they are most useful at the point where you have something to confirm,
which flows straight into [[Review]].

The usual mistake is drawing them as flowcharts, with one oval per screen or per function
call. A use case is a goal that leaves the actor better off, not a step.

Part of [[Modeling]]; UML also defines class, sequence, and state diagrams, which the vault
has no notes for.
